newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Albright sees Russia-NATO progress but questions.
newsitem.headline: Albright sees Russia-NATO progress but questions.

text.p: U.S. Secretary of State Madeleine Albright, on a whirlwind tour of world capitals, said on Friday the United States and Russia had made progress on a European security deal, but complex questions remained.

"I think that we have made some very important progress on this," she told a news conference, referring to a document that would define a new relationship between NATO and Russia as the alliance expands eastwards.
She added: "We are no longer in a situation of you versus us. We are all on the same side... The new NATO is not the NATO of the Cold War."
But it was clear that sticking points remained between NATO and Russia.

Moscow strongly opposes NATO plans to invite countries of central and eastern Europe to join. If the expansion must go ahead, the Kremlin says, the alliance should sign a legally binding document on ties with Russia, ceding some say to Moscow on future development.
Albright, on her first foreign trip since she became Secretary of State, has already visited NATO in Brussels, and the 11-day tour will also take her to Seoul, Tokyo and Beijing.

On Friday she became the first senior Western figure to visit Russian President Boris Yeltsin in the Kremlin this year, although Yeltsin received Palestinian leader Yasser Arafat there on Tuesday. Meetings with German Chancellor Helmut Kohl and French President Jacques Chirac have been held outside Moscow.
At Friday's meeting Yeltsin's face looked pale and waxen.

"I welcome you to the Kremlin, to Moscow, on this very responsible visit to work on certain problems that exist between us," said the president, recovering from heart surgery and pneumonia, as he sat down with Albright.

Russian Foreign Minister Yevgeny Primakov, describing Albright as "an iron lady but a very constructive lady", told the joint news conference a deal between Russia and NATO should have a "binding character".
"We are still negatively disposed to NATO expansion but we are also trying to do everything possible to minimise the complications that may arise if expansion goes ahead," he said.

"From Russia's point of view, any agreement, charter, document...whatever you want to call it, must have a binding character for both sides and, as far as I understand, Mrs Albright agreed with this."
But Albright did not address this point and her spokesman Nicholas Burns later told reporters that Washington still believed the agreement should not be legally binding.
A promise to make a document legally binding would have been a substantial concession by Washington, which might effectively have given Moscow veto powers over NATO decision-making.
Russia has warned NATO that its plans to grant membership to some of Moscow's Cold War allies in central and eastern Europe could upset the European security balance.
But after NATO made clear it would not change its plans to cope with Russian objections, Moscow has concentrated on negotiating a deal which would guarantee its security interests.
Moscow says a deal should include a NATO promise not to deploy nuclear forces and foreign troops on the territories of the new members.
Albright said NATO's nuclear weapons in Europe had been cut by 90 percent since the Cold War ended and the number of U.S. troops in Europe had dropped to 100,000 from 300,000 in 1989.
